Intelligence log (18 events)
  • 2023-12-01financing
    Gemini Data Center SD LLC acquired roughly 164 acres from Xcel Energy adjacent to Xcel Split Rock Substation in northeast Sioux Falls, laying groundwork for the proposed 500 MW Sioux Falls Technology Park. · source
  • 2025-08-06vote
    Sioux Falls City Council approved reclassifying the property from Tier III to Tier I growth-priority area, an unusual leapfrogging of the normal phased growth sequence. · source
  • 2025-08-15announcement
    SDPB reported LA-based Gemini Capital through Gemini Data Center SD LLC is seeking to build a hyperscale data center on land bought from Xcel Energy; project representative Kyle Peters confirmed an internal 500 MW capacity target contingent on state tax incentives. · source
  • 2025-10-07vote
    City Council voted 7-0 to annex approximately 164 acres east of Veterans Parkway for the Gemini project; city filed a notice of claim making Gemini responsible for future infrastructure costs if it walks away. · source
  • 2026-01-06hearing
    City Council held a nearly six-hour public hearing on the rezoning with overflow attendance; more than 50 speakers, mostly opposed, raised concerns about energy consumption, water use, electronic waste, and lack of community benefit. · source
  • 2026-01-06rezoning
    Council voted 7-0 to rezone roughly 145.6 acres from agricultural to light industrial with conditions: 200-ft setback, ~17 acres conservation, closed-loop cooling, domestic-only water use, city noise standards. · source
  • 2026-01-08protest
    Following the rezoning vote, opponents shouted expletives and criticism at the dais, prompting a five-minute recess; local coverage captured the outrage. · source
  • 2026-01-10public-comment
    Grassroots group Let Sioux Falls Vote launched a petition drive seeking to force a citywide referendum on the rezoning, needing 6,704 valid signatures by January 29. · source
  • 2026-01-26coverage
    Reporting confirmed Gemini completed its interconnection application and system impact study with Xcel Energy and is funding a facility study; a formal power agreement (subject to PUC review) still to be negotiated. · source
  • 2026-01-29filing
    Let Sioux Falls Vote submitted 378 petition sheets to the city clerk after more than 100 volunteers canvassed for 20 days in sub-zero temperatures. · source
  • 2026-01-30ruling
    City announced the referendum petition contained only 5,012 valid signatures, about 1,700 short of the 6,704 required; the petition was rejected and the rezoning remained in effect. · source
  • 2026-02-04vote
    SD House State Affairs Committee voted 9-3 to kill HB 1005, which would have granted data centers a 50-year sales-and-use tax exemption; an amendment offering a tiered 10-35 year exemption also failed. · source
  • 2026-02-18vote
    SD Senate committee advanced SB 135, the Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens, requiring large data centers to cover costs tied to meeting their power demands including exit costs if a project falls through. · source
  • 2026-02-19lawsuit
    A1 Development Solutions (Gemini local consulting firm) sued its own project representative Kyle Peters (Gov. Noem son-in-law) alleging he covertly diverted the data-center client and others while still under contract. · source
  • 2026-02-20vote
    SD Senate passed SB 135 34-0 after striking language that would have banned state/local tax exemptions for data centers. · source
  • 2026-03-02coverage
    Gemini launched a public website for the Sioux Falls Technology Park describing Gemini Family Office role in land ownership, planning, permitting, and coordination. · source
  • 2026-03-05vote
    SD House passed SB 135 60-7 with amendment applying the law to data centers with 10 MW or greater peak electrical use, requiring those projects to cover power-demand costs. · source
  • 2026-03-30incentive
    Governor signed SB 135, the Data Center Bill of Rights, into law — statewide cost-protection rules for large data center power demands (10 MW+) applicable to the Gemini project eventual Xcel service agreement. · source

Metrobloks Martindale-Brightwood Approved

Martindale-Brightwood (Indianapolis), IN · 14 ac · Operator: Metrobloks · Owner: Metrobloks

$500M, two-building, ~168,000 sq ft data-center campus at 2505 N. Sherman Ave. on the site of a long-abandoned drive-in theater, in a neighborhood with a documented history of lead-contaminated soil. Uses a closed-loop cooling system (water added once, then recirculated) and buys power from AES Indiana rather than the residential grid. MDC approved 3 variances + a rezoning 6-2 on April 1, 2026; City-County Council gave final rezoning approval May 4, 2026. Exempted from the Aug. 19, 2026 citywide moratorium as a previously-approved project. Residents' group Protect Martindale Brightwood said it was exploring legal options to challenge the approval. District councilor Ron Gibson's home was shot 13 times on April 7, 2026, days after he publicly backed the project; a note reading 'No Data Centers' was left at the scene.

Next step: Approved — pivot from stopping it to a binding CBA: enforceable caps on noise, water and cost, plus a community benefit.

Intelligence log (12 events)
  • 2025-12-18announcement
    Seattle-based Sabey Data Centers sought city approval for a roughly 130-acre, two-building data center campus on industrially-zoned land near Camby Road and Kentucky Avenue in Decatur Township, telling residents the project could generate more than $20M/year in property tax revenue at full buildout. · source
  • 2025-12-18public-comment
    Residents packed a Decatur Township Civic Council meeting at Decatur Central High School to question Sabey CEO John Sabey about the proposed data center; no speaker during public comment supported the project. · source
  • 2026-01-29hearing
    The Metropolitan Development Commission's hearing examiner held a petition hearing on Sabey's request for a variance of use to allow the data center campus on industrially-zoned land in Decatur Township. · source
  • 2026-02-26hearing
    The MDC hearing examiner recommended approval of Sabey's 130-acre Decatur Township data center proposal, advancing it to the full commission despite community opposition. · source
  • 2026-02-26protest
    About 90 Decatur Township residents demonstrated outside the City-County Building against the Sabey data center, citing noise, energy demand, water use, and property-value concerns; 1,400+ had signed an opposition petition vs. 24 supporters. · source
  • 2026-03-18vote
    The Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission voted to approve Sabey's variance-of-use request for a $4B, two-building, 900,000+ sq ft, ~250MW data center campus on 130 acres, making it Indianapolis's first hyperscale data center. · source
  • 2026-04-17lawsuit
    The Decatur Township Civic Council and more than half a dozen residents filed a petition for judicial review in Marion County Superior Court to overturn the MDC's approval, arguing the variance violated state law and due-process rights and amounted to a 'disguised rezoning.' · source

  • 2026-08-10moratorium

Joplin (Jasper County), MO · 600 MW · Operator: ReLoad (Scale Microgrids) · Filing LLC: Wildwood Ranch, LLC

Joplin annexed 540 acres and rezoned roughly 600 acres to heavy industrial for a gigawatt-scale campus with a co-located gas plant. A Wildwood Ranch homeowner is suing to void the rezoning, and an opposition group is pushing a 12-month moratorium.

Next step: Approved — pivot from stopping it to a binding CBA: enforceable caps on noise, water and cost, plus a community benefit.

  • 2024-12-23filing

  • 2025-10-01filing

State environmental permits

Backup generators, water withdrawal and stormwater are permitted by the state, usually earlier and in more detail than anything filed locally.

  • Texas TCEQ — Air Permits DivisionThe program page: which permits this state requires, and the office that issues them.

County & town filings

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

  • Search Fort Stockton (Pecos County) planning filingssearchPlanning departments post application files under many different names. Find the department, then ask the clerk for the application number — that number unlocks everything else.
  • Search Fort Stockton (Pecos County) property records / GISsearchThe parcel record names the buying LLC and the sale date, which is what ties an anonymous filing to an operator.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • ERCOT (Texas) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Public Utility Commission of Texas — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site. This project's locality centres on 30.890, -102.880 — search that point with a 5-mile radius.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

  • 2025-05-21coverage

  • 2025-06-04coverage

  • ERCOT (Texas) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Public Utility Commission of Texas — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

These are places to look, not evidence that anything has been filed. Links were checked on 2026-08-21; search links are queries, not records. What to ask for.

  • 2026-02-09announcement
    Constellation's Calpine unit and CyrusOne announced a Powered Land Capabilities agreement supplying 380MW for Phase 1 of a new data center adjacent to the Freestone Energy Center, with an exclusive option for an additional 380MW in Phase 2 (760MW total). · source
  • 2026-05-13public-comment
    A public notice regarding the data center project and upcoming county hearing was published in the Freestone County Times. · source
  • 2026-05-25protest
    A Change.org petition titled "Ban Data Centers in Freestone County" was started, citing water, noise and light pollution, rising power costs, and health/traffic impacts; it drew hundreds of signatures ahead of the county's June hearings. · source
  • 2026-06-03public-comment
    A Freestone County Commissioners Court meeting drew an overflow crowd (relocated to the District Courtroom) with 15+ residents raising concerns about permanent water loss, noise, health effects, and lack of transparency; resident Toni Abram asked for a 1-2 year pause, and the court scheduled a special meeting for June 10 and a public hearing for June 17. · source

Intelligence log (11 events)
  • 2024-06-13filing
    DataBank registered its first Red Oak building, DFW9 (425,170 sq ft, two-story data center with office space, $256M estimated cost), with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TABS project TABS2024020821). · source
  • 2024-09-10announcement
    DataBank announced development of a 480MW, 292-acre, eight-building data center campus in Red Oak, Ellis County, Texas (its third new-campus announcement in 12 months), with Phase 1 covering four buildings and a 400MW Oncor substation delivering 240MW of critical IT power; initial ready-for-service targeted for Q2 2026. · source
  • 2024-11-05filing
    DataBank filed plans for a second Red Oak building, DFW10 ($256M, 425,000+ sq ft), with construction slated to begin February 2025 and complete by mid-2028; report described it as a $256M addition to the growing Red Oak campus. · source
  • 2024-11-05filing
    Dallas Express reported DataBank's $265M expansion of the Red Oak campus (second facility), a 425,000 sq ft two-story building designed by JHET Architects, with construction beginning February 2025 and completion expected July 2028; full build-out envisions eight buildings totaling 3.4M+ sq ft. · source
  • 2025-12-01construction
    Construction work on DFW11 at the Red Oak campus began (per reported December 2025–January 2028 build schedule), part of the campus's staggered build-out following DFW9 and DFW10. · source
  • 2026-04-21financing
    DataBank closed a $2.0 billion construction loan — its largest financing to date, led by MUFG Bank under DataBank's Green Financing Framework — to fund the first three Red Oak buildings (DFW9, DFW10, DFW11: 600,000 sq ft, 180MW), all fully leased to an AI/cloud tenant (reported to be Oracle); the financing was said to accelerate delivery by about 18 months. · source
  • 2026-05-11hearing
    Red Oak Planning & Zoning Commission and City Council held a separate, contentious public hearing on an unrelated 830-acre Compass Datacenters project elsewhere in Red Oak; over 150 residents attended amid a 1,600-signature opposition petition citing noise, water, traffic and power-grid concerns (noted here for context but distinct from DataBank's Stainback Road campus). · source
  • 2026-06-01construction
    Reporting described DataBank's Red Oak campus in active construction, with initial concrete pours underway and electrical systems installation beginning; residents voiced mixed reactions including concerns about noise and water use, while DataBank held public meetings and appointed a community liaison. · source
  • 2026-06-16financing
    DataBank closed $1.45 billion in new financing across two transactions: an $800M corporate revolving credit facility and a $650M upsize (including DataBank's first private-placement notes) of the Red Oak construction loan to fund a fourth building (60MW additional IT capacity), bringing total Red Oak campus financing to $2.65 billion. · source
  • 2026-08-01construction
    Dallas Morning News reported DFW9 was expected to come online in August 2026, with DFW10 (interior work, ~$301M, completion January 2027) and DFW11 (~$315M, completion March 2027) following on a staggered schedule; residents cited concerns about scale, infrastructure strain, a 10-year tax-abatement delay on community benefits, and limited local job creation relative to project size. · source
  • 2026-08-11moratorium
    Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide audit of all data centers connecting to the ERCOT grid, effectively pausing new interconnections pending review — a state-level action affecting all Texas data center projects, including those on DataBank's Red Oak campus. · source

Google Berkeley County Under construction

Berkeley County, SC · — · Operator: Google · Owner: Google

$9B multi-site data center investment in Berkeley County, South Carolina. Under construction.

Intelligence log (18 events)
  • 2007-01-01announcement
    Google announces plans to construct a data center complex in Berkeley County, SC (Mount Holly Commerce Park, Moncks Corner) — its first South Carolina site, initial investment around $600 million. · source
  • 2010-11-01announcement
    Google announces plans to build a second building at the Berkeley County site. · source
  • 2010-12-01incentive
    Fee-in-Lieu of Tax (FILOT) agreement formalized, cutting Google property-tax assessment rate from 10.5% to 4% and locking it in for up to 50 years with an 80% rebate on the fee. · source
  • 2013-01-01announcement
    Google announces a further $600 million expansion, bringing cumulative Berkeley County investment to about $1.2 billion. · source
  • 2015-11-01permit
    Google receives a state permit to withdraw up to 183 million gallons per year of groundwater from the Charleston/Middendorf aquifer. · source
  • 2016-06-01filing
    Google reapplies to DHEC seeking to roughly triple its groundwater withdrawal permit to about 549 million gallons per year. · source
  • 2018-08-28incentive
    Berkeley County approves a tax-incentive package for a $600 million expansion (entity Maguro Enterprises), maintaining the 4% assessment/80% rebate FILOT structure; investment total reaches $2.4 billion. · source
  • 2019-02-01filing
    Google reapplies to DHEC for the 549-million-gallon-per-year groundwater withdrawal permit from the Middendorf aquifer. · source
  • 2019-08-22permit
    DHEC issues a draft permit allowing withdrawal of 549 million gallons of groundwater per year, drawing formal objections from the Coastal Conservation League and local water utilities. · source
  • 2019-12-12ruling
    Google, DHEC, the Coastal Conservation League and SELC reach a final agreement imposing tougher conditions: Google must treat groundwater as a last resort, develop alternative sources, and report usage quarterly. · source
  • 2023-01-01coverage
    A Google affiliate (Arum Composites LLC) purchases roughly 143 acres across five parcels in Berkeley County for about $28.5 million. · source
  • 2024-03-01permit
    Google seeks a land-disturbance permit for its second data center site in rural Dorchester County (Pine Hill Business Campus). · source
  • 2024-09-26announcement
    Google announces a combined $3.3 billion investment in SC: $2 billion for two new Dorchester County campuses and $1.3 billion to expand Berkeley County; includes $2.2 million for environmental initiatives. · source
  • 2024-09-26construction
    Groundbreaking ceremony held in Dorchester County with Governor McMaster; each new site expected to employ about 100 workers, existing Berkeley County site employs roughly 900. · source
  • 2024-10-15public-comment
    Public input meeting on emergency generators for the Pine Hill campus; about eight residents raised concerns over air quality, traffic, wetland impacts, and transparency. · source
  • 2025-10-13announcement
    Google announces a new $9 billion investment through 2027 to expand Berkeley County and continue Dorchester County construction — the largest single investment in South Carolina history. · source
  • 2025-12-01coverage
    Analysis examines whether Google $9 billion SC buildout is a net boon or burden for host communities, covering tax-incentive costs versus benefits. · source
  • 2026-04-24report
    SC Daily Gazette reports South Carolina data centers received a combined $828 million in state tax breaks on electricity and computer-equipment purchases in the prior year. · source

Intelligence log (16 events)
  • 2019-01-01filing
    Vistra/Luminant Mining conveyed roughly 5,000 acres of the former Thermo lignite mine to the City of Sulphur Springs; the deed included a restrictive covenant barring power generation or storage on the land. · source
  • 2025-02-01construction
    Phase I construction begins on the Matrix Data Center Campus: site grading, Trinity Road work, and utility infrastructure ahead of the eight-building, 800MW first phase. · source
  • 2025-06-13construction
    MSB Global holds official groundbreaking ceremony for the Matrix Data Center Campus, an 1,677-acre, up to 3GW, $18.7B hyperscale AI campus billed as a public-private partnership with the City of Sulphur Springs and Hopkins County. · source
  • 2025-09-30filing
    Vistra sends Sulphur Springs a cease-and-desist letter asserting the 2019 deed restrictive covenant bars on-site power generation/storage needed for the data center campus. · source
  • 2025-10-15lawsuit
    City of Sulphur Springs sues Vistra and Luminant Mining, arguing the restrictive covenant is unenforceable and against public policy; Vistra counters the covenant was known to the city. · source
  • 2025-11-01filing
    Texas AG Ken Paxton files an amicus brief supporting the City, revealing an Antitrust Division investigation into Luminant for inserting the same power-generation restrictive covenant into roughly 150 deeds across 18 Texas counties, calling it an attempt to improperly enrich Luminant by nearly $15 billion. · source
  • 2025-11-25filing
    Vistra and Luminant file their First Amended Answer and Counterclaims in Hopkins County (Cause No. CV45943), escalating the legal battle over the data center site. · source
  • 2026-01-21hearing
    Hopkins County District Court hearing; City Manager Marc Maxwell is subpoenaed by Vistra counsel and testifies; residents publicly press officials for answers on the project. · source
  • 2026-02-10ruling
    Judge Dan Moore denies a major City motion and issues a temporary injunction freezing new construction/development on the ~5,000-acre site pending trial, effectively halting power-system construction. · source
  • 2026-04-15lawsuit
    Resident Jack Curtis files suit alleging the City Council violated the Texas Open Meetings Act by concealing data-center deal details in council minutes/agendas. · source
  • 2026-05-06vote
    Sulphur Springs City Council authorizes $1.2 million in legal funding for the ongoing data-center litigation; residents protest the spending at the meeting. · source
  • 2026-05-06protest
    Residents protest outside the Sulphur Springs City Council meeting over the $1.2 million legal-cost allocation, citing lack of transparency. · source
  • 2026-06-03announcement
    At a packed City Council meeting, Mayor Tyler Law announces a new developer will take over the Matrix Data Center Campus, with original developer MSB Global being phased out amid the legal battles. · source
  • 2026-07-07hearing
    Judge Dan Moore hears over three hours of arguments on Vistra Rule 91a motion to dismiss 6 of 11 counts, focused on fraud allegations and when the city became aware of the deed restrictive covenant; no ruling issued. · source
  • 2026-07-18protest
    Sulphur Springs residents hold a peaceful demonstration against the data center as part of a coordinated nationwide National Day of Protest organized by advocacy group Humans First. · source
  • 2026-08-01coverage
    Heatmap News reports the trial original September 2026 date has been cancelled/pushed back, with the case now likely heading to trial in 2027. · source

County & town filings

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

  • Search Beaver Dam planning filingssearchPlanning departments post application files under many different names. Find the department, then ask the clerk for the application number — that number unlocks everything else.
  • Search Beaver Dam property records / GISsearchThe parcel record names the buying LLC and the sale date, which is what ties an anonymous filing to an operator.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • MISO (Midwest & Gulf) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Public Service Commission of Wisconsin — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

  • 2026-03-04vote
    Middlesex Township Board unanimously approves construction of a 450 MW electrical substation; PPL Electric Utilities confirms it can meet the full 1.35 GW peak demand with planned upgrades. · source
  • 2026-03-05construction
    Construction resumes on the $15 billion PAX-1 project following the substation approval. · source
  • 2026-04-01construction
    Two weeks of scheduled underground construction blasting begin at the PAX-1 site, twice daily on weekdays; nearby Country Manor West residents report feeling and hearing the blasts. · source
  • 2026-04-15coverage
    State Rep. Joe Webster begins advocating for new state oversight of data center projects including legislation requiring water-usage disclosure, amid resident complaints about PAX-1 construction noise, blasting, and well-water impacts. · source
  • 2026-04-20public-comment
    A planned town hall on data centers with State Rep. Barb Gleim (R-Cumberland) is canceled after overwhelming resident interest exceeded the space; residents say it felt like officials did not want to hear their concerns. · source
  • 2026-04-25public-comment
    Cumberland County Planning Department issues a review report recommending Middlesex Township deny an expansion of the data center overlay district and update its outdated 2003 comprehensive plan before amending zoning further. · source
  • 2026-04-29public-comment
    Cumberland County Planning Commission, Dickinson College, and CAEDC host a virtual data-center informational session drawing 230 pre-registration questions and 118 live, reflecting intense public interest. · source
  • 2026-06-25vote
    Pennsylvania House votes 197-5 to pass HB 2198 repealing the Computer Data Center Equipment sales-tax incentive, projected to cost $188.4 million in FY2026-27 growing to $517 million by 2030. · source
  • 2026-06-25vote
    Pennsylvania Senate passes HB 1667 containing the same data center tax incentive repeal by a vote of 44-6. · source
  • 2026-08-05hearing
    Middlesex Township supervisors cancel a planned vote to approve final construction of a PAX-1 building after more than 150 residents pack the municipal building beyond capacity, creating a fire hazard; rescheduled to August 19 at a school gym. · source
  • 2026-08-05protest
    Cumberland County residents organized by Neighbors Against PAX-1 rally against the data center, arguing the developer helped write the zoning ordinance in a way that handcuffs the township ability to impose conditions. · source
  • 2026-08-06lawsuit
    Ten Middlesex residents (Neighbors Against PAX-1 / Stop PAX-1) file a substantive validity/spot-zoning legal challenge alleging the 2025 data center overlay ordinance was effectively written by PAX-1 developers and approved via illegal spot zoning. · source
  • 2026-08-13lawsuit
    Opponents file a separate appeal with the PA Environmental Hearing Board challenging a stormwater permit for the PAX-1 site, arguing it was written for a 58-house residential subdivision rather than a hyperscale data center. · source
  • 2026-08-18incentive
    Gov. Shapiro signs a statewide executive order restricting data center development: requiring local approval for state permits, removing data centers from fast-track permitting, mandating CBAs, binding environmental/transparency commitments, and that projects secure their own electricity supply. · source
  • 2026-08-19hearing
    Rescheduled Middlesex Township supervisors meeting on PAX-1 building approval postponed a second time (moved to September 2) after a township official suffers a medical episode during the meeting. · source

State environmental permits

Backup generators, water withdrawal and stormwater are permitted by the state, usually earlier and in more detail than anything filed locally.

  • Pennsylvania DEPThe program page: which permits this state requires, and the office that issues them.
  • DEP Data Center Permit Tracker (the only state register built for data centers — it already feeds this tracker)Searchable public filings — search the operator, the shell LLC on the deed, and the address.

County & town filings

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

  • Search Cumberland County planning filingssearchPlanning departments post application files under many different names. Find the department, then ask the clerk for the application number — that number unlocks everything else.
  • Search Cumberland County property records / GISsearchThe parcel record names the buying LLC and the sale date, which is what ties an anonymous filing to an operator.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • PJM Interconnection (Mid-Atlantic, Ohio Valley) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

These are places to look, not evidence that anything has been filed. Links were checked on 2026-08-21; search links are queries, not records. What to ask for.

AWS Northern Indiana expansion (New Carlisle) Operating

New Carlisle (St. Joseph County), IN · 2,400 MW · Operator: Amazon (AWS) · Owner: Amazon · Tenant: AWS

Amazon plans a $15B investment in new Northern Indiana data center campuses, additional to the $11B investment announced the prior year in St. Joseph County, where its New Carlisle data center already operates. Amazon secures 2.4 GW for its needs (3 GW total new grid capacity) and, through NIPSCO Generation LLC arrangements, will pay to use existing power lines and cover new power plant costs. Amazon says the expansion creates 1,100+ direct high-skilled jobs.

  • 2024-04-25announcement
    Governor Holcomb announced that Amazon Web Services would invest $11 billion to build a data center campus at the Indiana Enterprise Center near New Carlisle, creating at least 1,000 jobs — the largest capital investment in Indiana history. · source
  • 2024-08-13vote
    St. Joseph County Council voted 7-2 to approve a 10-year 50% property tax abatement and a 35-year enterprise technology exemption (85% on data center equipment) for Amazon; the package included a $143 million community enhancement agreement for parks, schools, fire departments, and infrastructure. · source
  • 2024-09-30construction

  • 2025-08-13ruling
    IDEM cited Amazon for impacting nearly one acre of wetlands without authorization at the New Carlisle campus, ordered construction in state waters to cease, and required Amazon to withdraw its January 2025 permit application and resubmit with an additional 30% mitigation requirement. · source

  • 2025-09-24ruling
    The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved NiSource's petition to create NIPSCO Generation LLC (GenCo), a first-in-the-nation subsidiary utility to own, build, and manage generation assets exclusively for data centers in Northern Indiana, shielding existing NIPSCO retail customers from related costs. · source
  • 2025-10-29operational
    Amazon announced that Project Rainier, its $11 billion data center campus in New Carlisle dedicated to training Anthropic's Claude AI models on approximately 500,000 Trainium2 chips, was now operational; CNBC reported it as the company's biggest AI data center. · source
  • 2025-11-24announcement
    Amazon announced an additional $15 billion investment to build new data center campuses in Northern Indiana, adding up to 3 GW of capacity; NIPSCO would supply power under a 15-year contract beginning January 2027, with GenCo planning two 1.3 GW gas plants and 400 MW of battery storage. · source
  • 2026-06-24report
    Four Republican St. Joseph County Council members sent a letter to Amazon requesting voluntary contributions toward homeowner property tax relief, noting AWS had nearly $38 million in abated property taxes in the first half of 2026 alone. · source
  • 2026-07-10coverage
    Indiana Citizen reported that the New Carlisle campus had 935 full-time employees as of December 2025 (average $40.99/hour), with construction traffic more than doubling the town's population daily at peak; Amazon requested permanent filling of over 9 acres of wetlands and rerouting of 5,000 feet of streams. · source
  • 2026-07-23construction

  • 2024-08-13incentive

  • 2025-11-25filing

  • 2026-03-30coverage

State environmental permits

Backup generators, water withdrawal and stormwater are permitted by the state, usually earlier and in more detail than anything filed locally.

  • Indiana IDEM — Office of Air QualityThe program page: which permits this state requires, and the office that issues them.
  • IDEM Virtual File CabinetSearchable public filings — search the operator, the shell LLC on the deed, and the address.

County & town filings

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

  • Search New Carlisle planning filingssearchPlanning departments post application files under many different names. Find the department, then ask the clerk for the application number — that number unlocks everything else.
  • Search New Carlisle property records / GISsearchThe parcel record names the buying LLC and the sale date, which is what ties an anonymous filing to an operator.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • MISO (Midwest & Gulf) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • PJM Interconnection (Mid-Atlantic, Ohio Valley) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site. This project's locality centres on 41.700, -86.510 — search that point with a 5-mile radius.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

    Aurora City Council approved the Memorandum of Reimbursement with CyrusOne for the 2725 Bilter Road site. · source
  • 2024-10-02construction
    Governor JB Pritzker, Aurora Mayor Richard Irvin, and CyrusOne CEO Eric Schwartz held a groundbreaking ceremony for a $350 million, two-building (446,000 sq ft), 40 MW data center campus on Bilter Road, expected to open in early 2026. · source
  • 2024-10-03incentive
    Coverage confirmed the project was approved under the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity data center investment incentive program and includes a Project Labor Agreement with IBEW. · source
  • 2025-04-01utility

  • 2025-05-20utility

  • 2025-05-21filing

  • 2025-09-25moratorium

  • 2026-03-24vote
    As its 180-day moratorium expired, Aurora City Council approved strict siting and performance rules on new data centers: mandatory noise/water/sound studies, daytime/nighttime decibel caps (56/46 dB), and generators/chillers set back 1,500 feet from homes. · source
  • 2026-07-09coverage
    Residents near the CyrusOne Aurora data center said noise (measured around 80 decibels) continued disrupting daily life despite the company rooftop sound wall and ComEd-partnered generator-runtime reductions. · source
  • 2026-08-03coverage

  • 2024-01-01operational

  • 2025-05-01construction
    ABC7 Amarillo reported that construction on the Armstrong County data center began by Crusoe Energy in May 2025, with completion anticipated by late 2028 or early 2029. · source
  • 2025-10-01filing
    In late October 2025, Crusoe and Goodnight Wind submitted a co-location (net metering) proposal to the Public Utility Commission of Texas under SB 6, seeking to share a single interconnection point between the 265.5 MW wind farm and the first phase of the data center, Latitude Media reported. · source
  • 2025-10-17vote
    NewsChannel10 reported Armstrong County commissioners unanimously approved an amendment to Crusoe's tax abatement agreement, with the project scaled back from an original seven buildings on 350 acres to as few as three or four, and the county to receive $1.35 million per year per building in payments once each is operational. · source
  • 2025-11-14announcement
    Google CEO Sundar Pichai, alongside Governor Greg Abbott in Midlothian, announced a $40 billion Texas investment including a new data center in Armstrong County and two in Haskell County, the Texas Tribune reported. · source
  • 2025-11-24announcement

  • 2026-01-01filing
    Crusoe Energy filed a 465-page application with TCEQ in January 2026 to build a 933 MW off-grid natural gas power plant at the Goodnight campus designed to power at least two buildings, which could emit up to 4.5 million tons of CO2 per year, exceeding San Francisco's entire annual emissions, Yahoo/The Guardian reported. · source
  • 2026-03-15financing
    In mid-March 2026, Crusoe sold the wind-co-located portion of the Goodnight campus to Ensign Infrastructure, a Delaware-incorporated special purpose vehicle, Latitude Media reported. · source
  • 2026-03-18coverage

  • 2026-03-27ruling
    The Public Utility Commission of Texas adopted final net metering rules for co-located data centers of 75 MW or larger under SB 6, requiring mandatory emergency curtailment within 30 minutes and prohibiting co-located loads from demand response programs, Latitude Media reported on April 3. · source
  • 2026-04-02report
    Cleanview founder Michael Thomas reported that satellite imagery showed construction of Crusoe's 933 MW gas plant at the Goodnight campus was 'well underway,' calling it 'one of the first direct investments in fossil fuel infrastructure' by Google, as covered by Yahoo/The Guardian. · source
  • 2026-04-07filing
    Yahoo/The Guardian reported that Crusoe filed in January 2026 to build a 933 MW on-site natural gas power plant at the Goodnight campus that could emit up to 4.5 million tons of CO2 per year, and that Google spokesperson Chrissy Moy said 'We don't have a contract in place for the plant in Texas.' · source
  • 2026-07-30construction
    Construction Review Online reported the Goodnight campus (filed as GN DC1, LLC and internally called Project Llano) had grown to a $29 billion-plus, seven single-story-building project, with buildings 3 and 4 (about $500 million each) among those under construction and a nuclear-powered deployment targeted for 2027. · source

  • 2023-09-06construction
    Google broke ground on its $600 million Phase 1 data center in Mesa, its first physical presence in Arizona; Governor Katie Hobbs, Mayor John Giles, and Rep. Greg Stanton attended; Google announced the facility would be 100% air-cooled and donated $150,000 to Salt River Project for watershed restoration. · source
  • 2023-09-08coverage

  • 2024-04-09hearing

  • 2024-04-09coverage

  • 2025-07-01operational

  • 2025-07-08rezoning

  • 2025-10-14hearing

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • No organised market covers this statenoteThere is no public queue to read. The record is the utility's integrated resource plan and its filings at the PUC — plus FERC eLibrary for anything federally docketed.

  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

Intelligence log (23 events)
  • 2010-03-05incentive

    Microsoft established its first data center presence in Cheyenne, Wyoming. · source
  • 2014-01-01construction
    Microsoft expanded its original Cheyenne data center footprint, adding capacity to its existing campus. · source
  • 2021-01-01operational
    Microsoft opened two additional data centers in Cheyenne, further building out its Wyoming campus. · source
  • 2025-01-01incentive
    The Wyoming Legislature extended the state data-center sales-and-use tax exemption through 2042. · source
  • 2025-07-01construction
    Microsoft, with JE Dunn as general contractor, began heavy earthwork on a new data center campus on HR Ranch Road east of Cheyenne, with completion targeted for early 2026. · source
  • 2026-04-14announcement
    Microsoft announced intent to purchase roughly 3,200 acres in Cheyenne to roughly triple its data center footprint, pledging over $68 million in off-site infrastructure improvements and no reliance on local property tax incentives. · source
  • 2026-04-14utility
    Microsoft detailed a utility partnership with Black Hills Energy under the Large Power Contract Service (LPCS) tariff, under which Microsoft funds the full cost of electricity infrastructure so other ratepayers are not burdened. · source
  • 2026-04-14environmental
    Microsoft said it would minimize water use and fund replenishment projects in Cheyenne, with partners including Trout Unlimited, expected to restore an estimated 566 million gallons of water. · source
  • 2026-04-27protest
    Opposition to Cheyenne data center growth intensified as the city moved to accommodate further development, with residents raising sustained objections. · source
  • 2026-04-28hearing
    Angry Cheyenne residents spoke out at a public meeting against the proposed annexation and Microsoft data center project. · source
  • 2026-04-29report
    A Wyoming state legislator said the state needs to determine how revenue from the data center boom should be distributed among local governments and residents. · source
  • 2026-05-08environmental
    Wyoming residents pressed for clarity on where water for the expanding data center boom would come from in the semi-arid region. · source
  • 2026-05-27vote
    The Cheyenne City Council rejected a proposed 12-month moratorium on new data center development by an 8-1 vote after hours of debate over water, noise, and long-term community impacts. · source
  • 2026-05-28coverage
    Wyoming Public Media reported on the city council rejection of a data center moratorium, noting no pause on development despite resident concerns. · source
  • 2026-06-02hearing
    The Cheyenne Planning Commission held a five-hour hearing on Microsoft 3,200-acre southside expansion, recommending denial for most components. · source
  • 2026-06-05vote
    Microsoft data center annexation/zoning plans failed to secure the Cheyenne Planning Commission endorsement, with two parcels near Laramie County Community College falling short of the required votes. · source
  • 2026-06-12report
    Coverage explained Wyoming data center sales tax exemption, worth up to $22.6 million annually, and its extension through 2042. · source
  • 2026-07-06vote
    The Cheyenne City Council rejected a proposal to slow down the Microsoft land annexation process, clearing the way for a final vote. · source
  • 2026-07-13vote
    After a seven-hour public hearing with overwhelming resident opposition, the Cheyenne City Council passed Ordinance 4687 by a 6-3 vote, annexing roughly 3,460 acres into the city for Microsoft planned data center campus. · source
  • 2026-07-14coverage
    Reporting confirmed Cheyenne grew by 3,500 acres after the controversial Microsoft-related annexation vote following more than five hours of council discussion. · source
  • 2026-07-20protest
    Opponents launched a referendum petition drive seeking to reverse the Cheyenne City Council 3,460-acre annexation vote, needing roughly 2,700 signatures within 20 days. · source
  • 2026-08-07protest

    QTS purchased 615 acres in Fayetteville for $153.8 million (approximately $250,000 per acre) from the Fayette County Development Authority, brokered by CBRE, for what it called the world's largest multi-tenant data center campus. · source
  • 2022-09-19announcement
    QTS publicly announced Project Excalibur: a planned 6.6 million sq ft campus of 16 data center buildings plus 400,000 sq ft of office space on the 615-acre Fayetteville site, with construction to start in 2023 and full build-out by 2032, investing over $1 billion. · source
  • 2023-02-28permit
    Fayetteville Planning and Zoning Commission approved the conceptual site plan and schematic building elevations for the Excalibur Data Center after a 5-6 month Development of Regional Impact review involving GDOT and the Georgia Department of Community Affairs. · source

    Land clearing began at the QTS Project Excalibur site in April 2023, per Epoch AI satellite imagery analysis. · source
  • 2023-06-15permit
    Fayetteville City Council unanimously approved a development agreement between the City and National Acquisition Company, LLC (QTS affiliate) for the 612-acre data center campus at 1435 Highway 54 West. · source
  • 2024-03-19announcement
    The Fayette County Development Authority proposed 'Project Rita,' a 96 MW data center campus on 145.5 acres in Tyrone (adjacent to the QTS site), comprising two buildings totaling 490,000 sq ft with a requested Business Technology Park rezoning; the Town Council hearing was scheduled for March 21. · source
  • 2024-03-28vote
    Tyrone Town Council approved the rezoning for the Microsoft data center (Project Rita) on approximately 147 acres on North Highway 74, following Planning Commission and Town Council public hearings on February 22 and March 21 respectively. · source
  • 2025-05-01construction
    The first building on the QTS campus received its certificate of occupancy in May 2025, per the AJC, with a construction completion certificate issued September 25, 2025. · source
  • 2025-05-15report
    Fayette County Water System sent a letter to QTS revealing that a water meter installed during a system-wide smart-meter upgrade had not been read electronically, resulting in approximately 13 million gallons of unrecorded usage and a retroactive bill of approximately $147,000; the issue was discovered after a neighbor reported low water pressure. · source
  • 2025-10-01operational
    Microsoft's Fairwater 2 data center on the QTS campus began operations in October 2025, spanning more than 1 million sq ft and using closed-loop cooling described as consuming almost zero water. · source
  • 2025-11-12announcement
    Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the Fayetteville facility as part of the world's first AI superfactory, connecting the Atlanta Fairwater 2 site with Fairwater 1 in Wisconsin across a single flat network to train AI models at planet scale. · source
  • 2026-01-01moratorium
    In January 2026 Fayetteville City Council passed a 90-day moratorium on new data center development applications while working to revise the Unified Development Ordinance; City Manager Ray Gibson stated 'we do not want anymore data centers in our community.' · source
  • 2026-02-22coverage
    WBRC reported on community impacts from the QTS/Microsoft campus, with resident Diana Dietz citing heavy truck traffic on residential roads, transmission lines through neighborhoods, and concerns over rising power and water bills; QTS stated it uses water-free cooling and is committed to paying its fair share of power costs. · source
  • 2026-03-18withdrawal
    Crow Holdings Development withdrew its appeal of a denied data center project on Highway 85 North in Fayetteville one day before the scheduled City Council hearing; the city had also enacted UDO changes on March 5 that made data centers no longer permissible. · source
  • 2026-06-08financing
    QTS Fayetteville I DC1-2, LLC began sounding out investors for $5.4 billion in new debt ($4.9 billion secured bond plus $500 million term loan) to finance expansion of the Fayetteville campus leased to Microsoft, under an updated green bond framework with a PUE threshold tightened from 1.5 to 1.4. · source

State environmental permits

Backup generators, water withdrawal and stormwater are permitted by the state, usually earlier and in more detail than anything filed locally.

  • Texas TCEQ — Air Permits DivisionThe program page: which permits this state requires, and the office that issues them.
  • TCEQ Central RegistrySearchable public filings — search the operator, the shell LLC on the deed, and the address.

County & town filings

The rezoning application, site plan, traffic and noise studies, staff report and every revision.

  • Search Milam County planning filingssearchPlanning departments post application files under many different names. Find the department, then ask the clerk for the application number — that number unlocks everything else.
  • Search Milam County property records / GISsearchThe parcel record names the buying LLC and the sale date, which is what ties an anonymous filing to an operator.

Utility & grid records

The electricity request is filed with the grid operator and the utility long before the town hears about it — and states the real load.

  • ERCOT (Texas) — interconnection queueRequested megawatts, queue position and target in-service date. The MW here is the real number; the one at the town meeting is often phase one.
  • Public Utility Commission of Texas — docket searchSpecial contracts, large-load tariffs and rate cases are docketed here. Testimony and exhibits are public, and are usually more candid than the press release.
  • FERC eLibraryFederal filings: transmission agreements, interconnection service agreements, and co-location disputes.
  • Search the serving utility for a will-serve lettersearchThe will-serve or load-service letter is the utility's own written commitment. Ask the utility and the PUC for it by name — it is frequently the first document to exist.

Federal databases

Works anywhere, and covers the operator's record at its other sites.

  • EPA ECHO facility searchEvery federally-reported air, water and waste permit at a facility, plus its inspection and violation history. Search by address or draw a radius around the site. This project's locality centres on 30.750, -96.900 — search that point with a 5-mile radius.
  • EPA EnvirofactsThe same underlying records, queryable by county — useful for 'what else is permitted near this site' rather than one facility.
  • EPA Facility Registry ServiceResolves the shell LLC on a permit to the facility it belongs to. Worth a look when the filing name means nothing locally.

These are places to look, not evidence that anything has been filed. Links were checked on 2026-08-21; search links are queries, not records. What to ask for.

  • 2010-04-05announcement
    QTS announced plans to convert the former 210-acre Qimonda semiconductor plant in Sandston, VA into a data center campus, having acquired it through bankruptcy court for $12 million; the site included 1.3 million sq ft of buildings and 100 MW of power capacity. · source
  • 2010-11-03operational
    QTS opened the first 50,000 sq ft phase of its Richmond data center two months ahead of schedule, with up to 18 MW of power and an unnamed government agency as its first tenant. · source
  • 2011-03-16financing
    QTS announced it had invested $100 million in converting the former Qimonda site, with renovation about 5% complete and approximately 50 employees on site, projecting growth to 200 employees. · source
  • 2017-05-01operational
    In May 2017, QTS positioned Richmond as a hyperscale cloud campus, citing 110 MW from Dominion Virginia Power, 1.3 million sq ft across three buildings, and Henrico County's data center equipment tax rate reduction to $0.40 per $100 assessed value. · source
  • 2019-11-19filing
    QTS submitted plans to Henrico County for approximately 1.2 million sq ft of new data center space on a 73-acre parcel south of its main campus along Portugee Road, comprising three 330,000 sq ft buildings and one 165,000 sq ft facility. · source
  • 2021-06-07financing
    Blackstone announced it would acquire QTS Realty Trust for $78 per share in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately $10 billion including debt assumption, a 21% premium to the June 4 closing price. · source
  • 2022-07-13announcement
    QTS announced it had acquired 200 additional acres at its Richmond Mega Data Center campus for expansion of up to 240 MW across 1.5 million sq ft of new capacity at White Oak Technology Park. · source
  • 2023-12-01financing
    In December 2023, QTS purchased approximately 225 acres of land in Sandston for $18 million in initial transactions assembling the White Oak Technology Park II site. · source
  • 2024-05-01rezoning
    In May 2024, the Henrico County Board of Supervisors approved rezoning of 622 acres on both sides of East Williamsburg Road at Technology Boulevard for data center and manufacturing use, creating White Oak Technology Park II. · source
  • 2024-06-28financing
    QTS completed acquisition of approximately 397 acres from Hourigan LLC for $118.8 million, giving QTS control of all 622 acres of the rezoned White Oak Technology Park II site; Hourigan had purchased the parcels from Atlantic Crossing ($38.05M) and Vienna Finance ($20.5M) the same day. · source
  • 2024-09-01financing
    In September 2024, a QTS-affiliated LLC purchased approximately 98 acres from LL Flooring adjacent to the White Oak campus. · source
  • 2025-01-10rezoning
    Henrico County's new provisional use permit (PUP) requirement for all hyperscale data centers took effect, including in White Oak Technology Park, requiring board-level approval for new facilities that previously could proceed by right in industrial zones. · source
  • 2025-06-10vote
    The Henrico County Board of Supervisors approved new data center regulations including 500-foot tree buffers from residential areas, generator testing limits, mandatory equipment screening, and closed-loop cooling requirements; rules apply retroactively to rezoned projects without final site plan approval. · source

Intelligence log (13 events)
  • 2025-02-20announcement
    Valar Atomics emerged from stealth with a $19 million seed round led by Riot Ventures and announced plans to build small modular nuclear reactors, initially with a pilot site agreement in the Philippines. · source
  • 2025-06-18announcement
    U.S. Department of Energy issued a Request for Application for its Reactor Pilot Program, an expedited authorization pathway for advanced test reactors with a goal of at least three reactors reaching criticality by July 4, 2026. · source
  • 2025-07-08public-comment
    Emery County Commission hosted a town hall where Valar Atomics representatives answered citizen questions and safety concerns about the proposed Ward 250 test reactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab. · source
  • 2025-08-01announcement
    DOE announced Valar Atomics as one of 10 companies selected for its Reactor Pilot Program, authorizing construction and testing of the Ward 250 reactor at Utah San Rafael Energy Lab in Orangeville. · source
  • 2025-09-17construction
    Valar Atomics and the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab broke ground on the Ward 250 test reactor site in Orangeville, Emery County. · source
  • 2025-11-13financing
    Valar Atomics raised $130 million in Series A funding led by Snowpoint, Day One, and Dream Ventures, bringing total funding to over $150 million. · source
  • 2026-02-01permit
    Valar Atomics received preliminary Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) approval under the DOE Reactor Pilot Program for the Ward 250 test reactor. · source
  • 2026-02-15construction
    The Ward 250 reactor core was transported via three U.S. Air Force C-17 aircraft from March Air Reserve Base to Hill Air Force Base, then trucked to the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab, targeting operation by July 4, 2026. · source

    Emery County Commission approved a letter of support for Valar Atomics as the Ward 250 reactor arrived in the Castle Country region, citing job and tax base benefits. · source
  • 2026-04-23permit
    Valar Atomics received final Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) approval, clearing the way for power ascension testing of the Ward 250 reactor. · source
  • 2026-06-18operational
    Valar Atomics Ward 250 high-temperature gas reactor achieved zero-power criticality at the San Rafael Energy Lab, becoming the second reactor to go critical under the DOE Reactor Pilot Program and the first DOE-authorized reactor built entirely outside a national laboratory. · source
  • 2026-07-01announcement
    Valar Atomics and Nvidia announced a partnership to explore a 30-megawatt, nearly waterless AI data center in Orangeville powered by roughly six Ward-class reactors, using Nvidia DSX liquid-cooling technology; the Ward 250 also powered an Nvidia DGX Spark AI chip, a first for U.S. nuclear power. · source
  • 2026-08-03financing
    Valar Atomics raised a $1 billion Series B round led by Sequoia Capital (plus a $200 million credit facility), tripling its valuation to $6 billion, to fund mass production of factory-built nuclear reactors for AI data centers. · source

Montour County, PA · 800 ac · Operator: Talen Energy

County commissioners unanimously denied Talen Energy's request to rezone 800+ acres from agricultural to industrial for a data center plus power-plant expansion, after a grassroots group gathered ~3,000 petition signatures.

Next step: Denied — watch for a re-filing or a scaled-down resubmission; ask the clerk to add you to the notification list.

Source

Intelligence log (13 events)
  • 2024-11-01ruling
    FERC rejected a proposed interconnection service agreement among PJM, PPL Electric, and Talen that would have increased the load Talen could transfer directly from the Susquehanna nuclear plant to its co-located Amazon data center campus. · source
  • 2025-06-01utility
    Talen Energy expanded its Amazon Web Services partnership with a new long-term agreement to supply up to 1,920 MWe from its Susquehanna nuclear plant through 2042, part of Talen's broader co-location strategy for AI data centers in Pennsylvania. · source
  • 2025-08-01announcement
    Concerned Citizens of Montour County formed with four members after Talen's rezoning request became public; its first town hall days later drew about 120 people. · source
  • 2025-08-18filing
    Talen Energy submitted a rezoning petition to Montour County covering roughly 870 acres in Anthony and Derry Townships, seeking to change land from agricultural to industrial near its Montour Steam Electric Station for a data center and power-plant expansion. · source
  • 2025-11-19hearing
    The Montour County Planning Commission voted to recommend against Talen Energy's request to rezone roughly 870 acres of agricultural land to industrial. · source
  • 2026-01-23hearing
    Montour County commissioners held an all-day public hearing at First Baptist Church of Danville on Talen's rezoning request; residents wearing red 'Say No Industrial Rezoning' shirts testified about farmland loss, water use, noise, and land impact. · source
  • 2026-01-23public-comment
    Concerned Citizens of Montour County delivered a petition signed by about 3,000 residents opposing the rezoning, roughly twice the population of the township and more than voted there in the 2024 election. · source
  • 2026-02-10denial
    Montour County's three commissioners voted unanimously to deny Talen Energy's rezoning request; Chair Rebecca Dressler said Talen had not met its burden of proving the project would benefit the community and that no evidence showed benefits outweighed foreseeable public harms. · source
  • 2026-02-10coverage
    Talen Energy responded saying it remains committed to pursuing a data center in Montour County and would 'listen, incorporate feedback from the Commissioners, engage with the community, and refine our plans.' · source
  • 2026-03-30report
    Civil Eats profiled the Montour County fight as a case study of a small farm county organizing successfully against a hyperscale data center and power-plant expansion. · source
  • 2026-04-14public-comment
    Montour County held a public hearing on proposed amendments to its data center ordinance, including new height and setback distance requirements. · source
  • 2026-04-28ruling
    Montour County commissioners unanimously approved amended data center ordinance provisions establishing new height and setback requirements for any future data center development. · source
  • 2026-08-18moratorium
    Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order restricting data center development in Pennsylvania, eliminating fast-tracked permitting and formalizing GRID Standards requiring community engagement, energy-affordability protections, and environmental standards for developers seeking state support. · source

A1 Data Center (Millville) Blocked by ban

Millville, NJ · 1,400 MW · Ownership not yet identified

A 2.9 million sq ft campus on 66 acres, with building heights to 150 feet, that would have drawn roughly 1.4 GW from the grid - the largest data center proposal ever blocked in New Jersey. No site plan was ever formally submitted to the city; the Board of Commissioners banned data centers citywide first, on May 19, 2026, calling them incompatible with Millville's land use objectives, infrastructure capacity and community character. Millville borders Vineland, where the 300 MW DataOne/Nebius campus was already under construction. Opposition was organised by the Climate Revolution Action Network; Mayor Dan Dixon described the ordinance as proactive rather than a response to a specific application.

Next step: Blocked by a local ban or moratorium - the project stopped at the ordinance, not at an application. Watch for the ordinance being challenged in court or allowed to lapse.

Abei Energy data center proposal (rezoning request) Blocked by ban

Starke County, IN · — · Operator: Abei Energy (data center division)

Chicago-based Abei Energy's data center division emailed the Starke County Plan Commission asking about rezoning two parcels from Agricultural to Industrial. County officials disclosed the inquiry to residents on 2025-11-03; Abei was placed on the Plan Commission's 2025-11-12 agenda. Exact parcels, acreage, and project size were never disclosed publicly. The county drafted a hyperscale data center moratorium ordinance in direct response and adopted it (Ordinance 2025-37) on 2025-12-15, before Abei's proposal advanced to a rezoning vote -- so this project's outcome is 'moratorium' (blocked by the county's own timeout), not a formal denial.

Next step: Blocked by a local ban or moratorium - the project stopped at the ordinance, not at an application. Watch for the ordinance being challenged in court or allowed to lapse.

Decennial Group Akron Data Center Campus (proposed) Blocked by ban

Fulton County (Akron), IN · 500 MW · Operator: Decennial Group

Decennial Group co-founder David Pavlick (also spelled 'Pavlik' in some coverage) proposed a roughly 500 MW, 300-acre hyperscale data center campus near Akron, in Fulton County, no specific parcel/site was ever named publicly, and no hyperscale tenant was named (Pavlick said an unnamed hyperscale company larger than Decennial's existing CoreWeave-tenanted Hammond, IN facility was interested). The Fulton County Area Plan Commission recommended a 12-month moratorium 6-1 on Feb. 10, 2026 specifically in response to this proposal, and the Board of Commissioners adopted it 2-1 on March 2, 2026, effectively pausing the project. No later announcement of the project being formally withdrawn was located; it is currently blocked by the moratorium rather than confirmed dead.

Next step: Blocked by a local ban or moratorium - the project stopped at the ordinance, not at an application. Watch for the ordinance being challenged in court or allowed to lapse.

Intelligence log (19 events)
  • 2024-09-23filing
    Developer Sebastian Rucci registers Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC and related entities in California to pursue the Imperial County AI/ML data center project. · source
  • 2025-11-03filing

  • 2025-11-06environmental

  • 2026-05-01denial

  • 2026-06-04hearing

  • 2026-06-05lawsuit

  • 2026-06-16moratorium

The seven documents worth asking for

Every dossier above ends with Find the paper trail — the registers, dockets and queues that hold that project's record. This is what to look for once you are there, roughly in the order the documents tend to exist. A records request that arrives after the vote is worth nothing, so ask early and ask by name.

Air permit for the backup generators

Who holds it: State environmental agency (air quality division)

Plan approval / construction permit for the diesel or gas gensets, with the emissions inventory and run-hour limits.

Why it is worth having: The genset count and permitted run hours are the most reliable public proxy for the campus's real size — often filed before any MW figure is public, and usually larger than what the developer told the town.

Water withdrawal / supply agreement

Who holds it: State water authority, river basin commission, or the municipal water utility

Permitted withdrawal volume, the source, and any will-serve letter from the water utility.

Why it is worth having: Turns 'we use very little water' into a number on letterhead, and shows whether existing customers were modelled during a drought year.

NPDES / stormwater and discharge permits

Who holds it: State environmental agency (water division) or EPA region

Construction stormwater permit, erosion plan, and any cooling-blowdown discharge authorisation.

Why it is worth having: Earliest filing on most sites — often the first hard proof of acreage and grading before a rezoning is even docketed.

Rezoning / special-use application file

Who holds it: County or town planning department

The full application: site plan, traffic study, noise study, proffers, staff report, and every submitted revision.

Why it is worth having: The staff report names the conditions staff thought were necessary. Conditions dropped between versions are the single most productive thing to read aloud at a hearing.

Interconnection / large-load service request

Who holds it: Grid operator (RTO/ISO) and the serving utility

Queue position, requested MW, in-service date, and any network upgrades the project triggers.

Why it is worth having: Shows the real megawatts and who pays for the wires. A queue request far larger than the public figure is a phased build the community has not been told about.

Special contract / rate filing at the PUC

Who holds it: State public utility commission docket

Any special tariff, large-load class, or contract the utility filed to serve this customer, plus its cost allocation.

Why it is worth having: This is where it becomes visible whether other ratepayers subsidise the connection. Testimony and exhibits are public and usually more candid than the press release.

Tax abatement / incentive agreement

Who holds it: County, school district, IDA or state development authority

The PILOT or abatement resolution, the jobs and investment commitments, and any clawback terms.

Why it is worth having: Converts 'economic development' into the actual net revenue per year, and shows what happens if the promised jobs never appear.

These are places to look, not evidence that anything has been filed. Links were checked on 2026-08-21; search links are queries, not records.

size_mwPlanned IT/critical load in MW, or blank.
acresSite acreage, or blank.
announcedISO date first publicly proposed, or blank.
rezoning_filedISO date the rezoning/permit application was filed, or blank.
hearing_dateISO date of the next/decisive public hearing, or blank.
decided_dateISO date a terminal decision was reached, or blank.
outcomeapproved | denied | withdrawn | blank (blank = still live).
stageDERIVED status shown on the page (Hearing scheduled, Awaiting decision, In review, Proposed, Rumored, Approved, Under construction, Operating, Denied, Withdrawn, Blocked by ban).
days_to_hearingDERIVED days until the hearing (negative once past), or blank.
noteOne-line plain-language status.
sourcePrimary URL backing the current status.
as_ofISO date the source was read, or blank.
verifiedtrue if a source is on record.

Read stage, not outcome: stage is what applies today and is recomputed on every build. The JSON adds an events log per project that the CSV can't hold.

Report a project near you

A weekly scan of local news and known megaprojects surfaces leads into a review queue; a human reads the governing body's own agenda or the reporting before anything lands here, which is where each row's source and date come from. That means this is a working set, not a census — most of the country's activity isn't in here yet.
